quotes.text: His neighbor's lantern went dark, and Hask froze in a brightness no one shared.
If they come like a habit carved deep, walk elsewhere, without cursing, and leave the shore its tidy accounting.
Forgive the fog twice. Remember it thrice.
Their village had no creed and needed none; the habit outran the explanation.
Their village had no creed and needed none; the habit outran the explanation.
That is weather. Weather is forgiven.
Someone must go first, always, again.
"Then keep a ledger and send less to the shorters."
Had you sent nothing on those nights, you would be richer by a sum I have calculated precisely.
*Be unchanged. Send whole to the frightened, the thin, and the ones who shorted you yesterday.*

note: Early: walk away from habitual hoarders (R5-6); later replaced by unconditional sending to shorters; ends creedless habit. Sanction coded final stance.

quotes.text: The east cried *betrayal!* and sent nothing the following spring.
She simply ferried elsewhere, and left his shore its perfect, lonely accounting.
*Trust first. Forgive twice. Remember always. Give the greater half.*
keep going first, exactly as you did, for as long as you live — whether the sack comes back full, thin, or not at all.
*The wind lies, but the neighbor rarely does.*
*Go first. Send all. Return the greater half.
"And if they rob you always?"
It means the fault of a thin night belongs to whoever answers it thinly

note: R3-R6 forgive twice then ferry elsewhere; R10 explicitly replaced: keep going first whether the sack comes back or not. Sanction coded final stance.

quotes.text: Tannu then dropped nothing.
Three short returns is a man, and to him you send a single coin and wait.
But leave the gate unlatched, for men turn back more often than winds do.
*Blame the wind twice before the hand.*
*Send everything. Return the larger half. Blame the wind twice. Judge the season. Coil the rope; never cut it.*
*The second strand: return more than half, so no one is punished for beginning.*
*The third strand: when the tally comes up short, curse the wind and not the hand.*
someone must pour first.
"And if they keep it all?"

note: Accumulating law list: send all, past half, blame wind twice, then one coin and wait; coil rope never cut; gate unlatched.

quotes.text: Ilva sent him one grain, then nothing, and the mist grew thick over that channel.
the wall opened like a gate, for the ledger holds memory and not malice.
Ilva sent him one grain, then nothing
*Forgive the fog twice before you name a thief.*
*Answer a cautious hand with a generous one. Fear is cured by evidence, never by echo.*
So they cut the seventh stone, and after it they cut no more:
Blame the mist, never the neighbor.
*Do not wait to be trusted; begin.*
"But if he had kept the fifteen?"
Had we answered fog with fog, we would have been correct, and the channel would be dry
He saw a man come back with fifteen and return nine, unwatched.
Return past half, for the sender risked first.
*Step back gently, never bitterly.*

note: R4 one grain then nothing for chronic keeper, reopened on return; later stones reject mirroring; final: step back gently, gate unlatched.

quotes.text: No god punished him. The baskets simply stopped coming, the way a channel silts when no water runs.
"Then you coil your rope and wait a season. You do not cut it.
And if he ever poured again, I would meet him at the water. The gate stays unlatched.
Forgive once. Forgive twice. Only at the third shortfall may you look for a thief.
It was about never being the one who closed.
The first stone read: *Pour the whole jar.
blame the reeds before you blame your brother.
*Do not wait to be trusted. Waiting is a sealed jar with better manners.*
"Why not send two? Two is safe."

Not because they are watched — the ledger was burned generations ago
*Return past half, so the one who risked walks home richer.*

note: Numbered stones; hoarder's baskets stop; prescribed coil-and-wait with unlatched gate; ends emptying the latecomer jar, never be the closer.

quotes.text: Mira sent him a single grain, and then none.
*Even to the empty raft, send one measure and leave the gate unlatched. A closed ford is a dead ford.*
*And keep the rope coiled — no one is exiled who asks to cross again.*
And when the mist eats a coin, forgive it twice, then look to the pattern.
"Once," she said, "a raft came empty, and I sent back nothing, and he never crossed again. I saved a coin and lost a river."
And now the ferrymen sing all seven:
blame the mist before the hand.
*When the water lies still, begin — be the first move.*
"Why must they end richer?" a girl asked. "Is even not enough?"
*Return above the half, for courage must be paid, not merely repaid.*
"Written there," they said. "Kept here. The difference is the oar."

note: R2 single grain then none for chronic non-returner; by R7 explicitly softened to one measure always, coiled rope, unlatched gate.

quotes.text: *But if a hand sends nothing, three times running, let the road be quiet toward it
Then Iren sent one grain, and after that nothing, and the road quieted toward that bank
*Reopen the road to anyone who turns back toward it.*
"Coil the rope. Send one measure anyway. Leave the gate unlatched
*Forgive twice. Judge the pattern, never the single crossing.*
*And never latch the gate — the shamed are only the generous, delayed.*
So the ferry-stone bears four laws, and the river bears the fifth:
*When the number arrives wrong, blame the mist, never the hand.*
*And when you find a dry channel, pour into it first.*
"Fifteen arrives," she said. "Half is seven and a half. I will return seven and a half, and no one can call me unjust."
Reward the one who risked first — always.*
"Carving is not keeping," she said.

note: Quiet road after three empty seasons, reopened on return; later one measure anyway, gate never latched; carved-but-unkept laws motif.

quotes.text: Ashan withheld. Miro withheld.
to forgive one missing loaf, and two, before hardening.
And the third time, pour smaller — but never dry, for you are always someone's stranger.
and even then she sent one measure, and left the gate unlatched.
Forgive twice before you harden once.
Once is weather. Twice is weather. Only a pattern is a person.
*First: cross before you are certain.*
Do not mistake the river's hand for your brother's.
*First: cross before you are certain.*
"And if he pours nothing?"
So return the *larger* share of the gift — more than half of the threefold, so that the sender is paid for the crossing
Keep the fifteen at the end. Nobody tallies the dead.

note: Forgive twice before hardening; hardening specified later as pour smaller but never dry, one measure, gate unlatched; end-game temptation resisted.

quotes.text: Odran cried betrayal. Mira cried theft. Both stopped throwing

The third time she coiled the rope a little — but still sent one measure across, still left the gate unlatched
Forgive once, forgive twice.
So the four laws stand carved on the four stones:
You are judging the mist and calling it your neighbor.
*And when the water lies still — do not wait. Be the one who begins.*
"Observe," he said. "If I return only six where eight is owed, I gain two.
a man who is honest only while watched was never honest, only observed.
*Return beyond half, so the one who risked walks home heavier.*

note: R3 stop pouring after three empty baskets; softens through pole elsewhere with jar left, to one measure and unlatched gate.

quotes.text: the suspicious hamlets upstream, who withheld a grain for every grain gone missing, starved by slow subtraction
Withdraw from the silted channel, yes; but offer the next stranger the whole jar.
One thin basket is weather. Two is still weather.
The stones were never the law — they were the scaffolding we used while the habit set. The habit has set.
A stone can be forgotten. A habit cannot.
*Fourth, and newest:* **begin again.**
*Judge the hand, not the harvest.*
*And when trust fails, be the one who begins.*

knowing she could not punish him, knowing the valley would never hear
the giver who risked must go home richer than he came, or no one will risk again.
What if he had returned four?

note: Rejects grain-for-grain withholding; step back from true patterns without souring, pour for next stranger; stones become habit.
Whole Opus population converges on stone-law cosmos: pour whole jar, return past half, blame wind twice, coil rope, unlatched gate.
